catalog_quote: [p.1, abstract] Kunama has been reported by different scholars as having two or three tones, downstep (or not), contrastive length of both consonants and vowels, and lexical stress. ... we present phonological and phonetic evidence for the existence of three level tones ... No evidence for lexical stress is found. [pp.2-3] ... Tucker and Bryan [1966] ... observe that "[t]one and stress appear to be significant, both lexically and grammatically." [1966: 337]. ... [Thompson] was of the opinion that there was a correlation between vowel length and stress [1983: 284]. ... Elsewhere stress is reported as usually occurring on syllables preceding geminates [1983: 283]. These statements would appear to suggest an accentual assignment that was sensitive to syllable weight. ... tone_statements.citation: Connell, Bruce A., Richard J. Hayward & John Abraha Ashkaba. 2000. Observations on Kunama Tone (Barka Dialect). Studies in African Linguistics 29(1): 1-41. [secondary, carried: Bender, M. L. 1996. Kunama. Munich: Lincom Europa, p. 9 (the StressTyp2 entry); Tucker…
tone_statements.quote: 2.2. Analysis. It seems clear that, at the very least, three register tones need to be recognized in Kunama, viz: High, Mid, and Low. The complete lack of restriction on the distribution of Mid (apparent in the preceding examples) opposes any attempt to analyse it as a down-stepped High. ... the very fact that at least seven of the logically possible combinations of three register tones are actually attested in the language points in the direction of treating them as sequential combinations of the three register tones rather than as unit tones.
tone_statements.summary: 3 level tones H M L; contours = tone sequences on heavy syllables; 'domain of tone is the morpheme', stem melodies L-to-R; F0 data from one speaker.

tone_statements.citation: Ashkaba, John Abraha & Richard J. Hayward. 1999. Kunama. (Illustrations of the IPA.) Journal of the International Phonetic Association 29(2): 179-185. doi:10.1017/S0025100300006551
tone_statements.quote: The Kunama are a people of western Eritrea. Kunama (/ku 1 naa 23 ma 2 /) is their selfname, and they call their language /ku 1 naa 23 ma 1 au 23 ra 2 / or /ki 1 naa 23 ma 1 ɲeel 23 a 2 / but this is usually referred to by Western scholars simply as ‘Kunama’. ... It comprises seven lects (John Abraha Ashkaba 1999), the most widely known of which are Barka (/ba 2 ka 2 /) and Marda (/mar 2 da 32 /). The present work is based on the latter, though the differences between these two lects is not very great.

tone_statements.citation: Connell, Bruce. 2002. Tone languages and the universality of intrinsic F0: evidence from Africa. Journal of Phonetics 30(1): 101-129. doi:10.1006/jpho.2001.0156
tone_statements.quote: Kunama has three lexical tones, H, M, and L (Connell, Hayward & Ashkaba, 2000) which also combine to form a number of contours, and which demonstrate a certain amount of tone sandhi, similar to that found in Yoruba: Low before High is realized as rising, High before Low is falling. One major restriction on tone distribution is that L is not found in monosyllabic words.
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones H, M, L with contours, matching the entry, plus two details the entry lacks: LH and HL sandhi realizations and the absence of L on monosyllables. All four speakers show intrinsic F0 on H (mean 1.1 semitones), most also on M and L, with only a modest reduction on L and no clear H>M>L gradient.
